newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Indonesian soldier paid to kill Nobel winner - bishop.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian soldier paid to kill Nobel winner - bishop.

text.p: An Indonesian soldier was paid to assassinate Nobel Peace prize winner Bishop Carlos Belo on Christmas Eve but was stopped by suspicious Belo supporters who beat him to death, an Australian bishop said on Friday.

The Catholic Auxiliary Bishop of Melbourne, Hilton Deakin, said he had received a fax from a prominent East Timorese Roman Catholic detailing how the alleged assassination plot was uncovered and how the suspected assassin was killed.

The soldier, Corporal Alfredo dos Santos, was beaten to death on December 24. Residents said he had been found with a pistol in the grounds of Dili cathedral. Indonesian police said on Thursday they had detained 15 suspects in the killing.

Deakin, who has visited East Timor, told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio thousands of supporters welcoming Belo back to the cathedral in the territory's capital after a trip to Europe found a group of Indonesian soldiers outside.
One soldier was heard talking about how he would kill Belo, Deakin said. "Somebody had heard one of them speaking and saying derogatory things about the bishop and (how) he would get him, and so on.

"There was an awful scuffle... eventually a dead body was found inside the cathedral and, by all accounts, the smear of blood on the floor indicated the body had been dragged into the cathedral after the person had been severely wounded," he said.
"Hundreds of thousands of rupiahs ... equivalent to several thousand Australian dollars" were found on the body, he added.
Belo was not immediately available to comment on the report.
Deakin, who did not identify the fax sender, said it was believed the money was payment for the planned assassination of Belo, possibly the most popular man in East Timor.
The Indonesian military said the dead man, who was wearing civilian clothes, was off-duty and visiting the cathedral as a worshipper on his own accord.
Deakin said he had decided to release the details of the fax because he was concerned about the safety of Belo, who said last month attempts were made on his life in 1989 and 1991.

Belo, whose often strong stand against human rights abuses has earned him deep respect in the majority Catholic territory, has publicly apologised for the killing of the soldier, a native East Timorese and father of seven.

Indonesian troops invaded the former Portugese colony of East Timor in 1975 and made it Indonesia's 27th province in 1976. The move has not been recognised by the United Nations and mostly Moslem Indonesia maintains a large security force there in the face of continued political and armed resistance.
